P1.evidence: The closest to a genuine setter handoff in the batch — 'I've read over some of the notes from, it looks like you spoke to Kim on our team, and I got those details. So, really, we're just going to pick up where we left off with him' — but still no actual detail reflected back, so the prospect had to start from the beginning anyway. Frame two-part again: 'understand what's going on with your fitness right now. What are you looking to accomplish?' with no 'what's in the way' and no 'what you need'. Agreement asked and given. Open question ran clean.

P2.evidence: Training and diet were both genuinely well run. The rep mapped the current programme in detail — upper/lower split, four sets, eight exercises, three-minute rests, session length — and then asked the sharp question about results: 'why do you feel like it's not giving you more results? You've been doing it for a year and a half. Why do you think you still have the stomach fat?' Diet was properly chased too: 'Did they give you that plan, or did you just research that?' and 'what caused you to start tracking your macros a month ago?', producing the fat-versus-carb imbalance he had discovered. Against that, no age, no height, weight only volunteered inside the macro discussion, and occupation never asked at all — the rep established the schedule but never what the man does for a living, which also left the ICP occupation test unanswerable. No health conditions question and no injuries question anywhere. Sleep part-credits: bedtime was asked and 10 to 11pm established against a 5am wake, but quality was not. Energy never raised.

P3.evidence: The best-run P3 of the batch. The bridge question was asked, not understood, and then rephrased rather than abandoned — 'let's say that you worked with Trevor, you got your workouts down to 30 or 40 minutes a session, you started losing the weight... what would, if anything, would be different for you?' and then 'how did you see that affecting or helping other parts of your life, maybe?' — which is exactly P3d and P3e. P3f ran directly and productively: 'is anything coming up as a result of maybe you not spending as much time with them now?' produced the real friction, his wife saying 'hey, I need some help here with them... take them to the park... help them with the homeworks'. The reflect-back landed too: 'it sounds like the most important thing is, I guess, the wife happy and being there for your kids, obviously, but just finding a routine to do that.' What is missing is the last layer — no 'something you want to do but can't', and no drive through to identity or what kind of father he wants to be, which is where a man who lost eight years to his first child would have gone.

P4.evidence: The only phase in this batch to hit every check. Full history surfaced — six years of jiu jitsu, the eight-year stop after his eldest was born, the restart, why jiu jitsu failed the second time (commute plus 9pm classes plus socialising), and eighteen months of Fitness FAQs. The rep confirmed the pattern explicitly: 'So you were doing jujitsu, and then when your first daughter was born, you stopped? You stopped working out completely, and until just a year and a half ago?' He then established the structural gap precisely — 'you didn't really get any feedback or someone kind of like adjusting, okay, maybe increase the weights here or do more reps... any personalization?' → 'No, no, no, no' — and got the prospect to articulate the value of the alternative himself with 'What do you see the difference as, like, just a course or videos versus having someone actually customizing things, giving you feedback?', which produced 'it's personalized, real people, yeah, and I was impressed'. That is the phase working as designed.

P5.evidence: Absent for the sixth consecutive call in this batch. This is now unambiguously a systemic gap rather than a per-call lapse, and it is consistent with the sales manager instructing this rep the previous day to stop using consequence questions. The material here was fully assembled and untouched: a man who already lost eight years to inactivity once, whose wife is now asking for help he cannot give, who is finishing workouts after 10pm on a 5am start, and whose three children are 13, 7 and 3. Not one question about what the next two years look like if nothing changes.

P6.evidence: The belief check ran properly and, notably, the rep deferred the prospect's direct price question in order to run it — asked about cost, he said 'Yeah. Going to get there next. Just before we do...' and then asked 'how do you feel about it though? Like deep. Do you feel like that's what you're looking for? Or maybe not? Is it missing anything?' That is correct sequencing and the only instance of it in the batch. The all-in question never ran, so no genuine commitment existed before the number, only a soft 'I think it's kind of what I was looking for'. And when hesitation arrived the rep went down-market instead of returning to Phase 5.

P11.evidence: The rep did walk the onboarding sequence before pricing — 'we get you access into the app, get you into the trainings, you're going to submit an onboarding form, Trevor's going to look over that, and then you're going to book your onboarding call' — which is the right content in the right place, but delivered as a future-pace rather than executed. No payment was requested and no link was sent, so steps two to four could not run.

objection_plays.detail: Trigger explicit and repeated. The rep ran the value half of the isolate well — 'if we're talking about getting your time back for your kids and losing the weight and moving better, feeling better, eating better, do you feel like it would be worth it?' → 'I would say so. It will be a good investment' — which cleanly established the blocker was capacity, not value. Then the play stopped. No permission-to-be-honest question, no should-I-versus-how frame, and no financial picture at all: no cash on hand, no monthly surplus, no cards, no available credit, no investments. Instead he offered to 'find something lower', which is the opposite of the scripted move and which pre-emptively conceded the price.

Trigger present twice, including on the secondary product where the prospect had just said it was in his range. No move ran. The rep instead pre-labelled the objection as terminal: 'Usually it's a nice way to say no, it is what it is.' Telling a prospect that his stated intention to think about it is really a refusal ends the conversation rather than progressing it, and it ended a live opportunity on the $199 product.

The documented script gap, live and named: a cheaper alternative that is genuinely working. He has been on Fitness FAQs for eighteen months with real measurable progress, says so explicitly — 'It's not that I'm not seeing the results' — and named a specific substitute, Build Simple at $80-100 a month, as his budget range. Objection C assumes the blocker is capacity to pay rather than perceived value against a functioning low-cost substitute, so there was nothing to run. What the rep did instead made it worse: he questioned the prospect's seriousness ('It sounds like maybe you're, you know, maybe not at that point') and dismissed the substitute without argument ('seems like it's more of the same'). This is the second recorded instance of this gap after the Badrane Hriouch call and it needs a scripted answer.

notes: Technically the best discovery in the batch — the only phase-perfect P4, the best P3, and the only time the rep held back the price to run a belief check first — and it still lost, because there was no consequence frame and because the one objection that arrived is the one the playbook has no answer for. Two corrections: build a real value-versus-substitute argument for prospects already succeeding on a $80-200 programme, and never characterise a prospect's budget as a lack of seriousness — there was a live $199 sale on the table when the call was ended.
